cards.back: Extreme agitation, incoherent shouting, paranoia, apparent great strength, pain insensitivity, hyperthermia with clothing removal, and profuse sweating. Severe acidosis and hyperthermia cause sudden cardiac arrest, classically right after the struggle stops.

cards.front: How does pneumonia usually present in an adult versus an elder?
cards.back: Adult: fever, chills, productive cough, pleuritic chest pain, and crackles over one area. Elder: confusion, weakness or a fall, often without fever or cough.

cards.front: What is the classic sound and pattern of pertussis?
cards.back: Violent coughing fits that empty the lungs followed by a high-pitched whoop on inhalation, often with vomiting afterward. Infants may have apnea or cyanosis instead of a whoop.

cards.front: What age range and findings define croup?
cards.back: Roughly 6 months to 3 years. Viral, gradual over a day or two, worse at night, with a barking seal-like cough and inspiratory stridor. No drooling and not toxic appearing.

cards.front: What are the four hallmarks of epiglottitis and the one absolute rule?
cards.back: Sudden onset, high fever with a toxic appearance, drooling, and the tripod position with a muffled voice. The rule: put nothing in the mouth and do not inspect the throat.

cards.front: Why do thick secretions make cystic fibrosis patients chronically ill?
cards.back: Mucus too thick to clear plugs airways and breeds chronic lung infection, while thickened pancreatic secretions block digestive enzymes and cause malnutrition. Ask what is different from their baseline.

cards.front: How does cardiogenic pulmonary edema differ from pneumonia on lung sounds and history?
cards.back: Pulmonary edema gives crackles at both bases that rise, sudden onset often at night, no fever, and a heart failure history. Pneumonia gives crackles in one area with fever over days.

quiz.q: A 45-year-old has vague, crampy pain around the navel that over six hours has become a sharp pain he can point to in the right lower quadrant. What has happened?
choices: The pain is now referred from the gallbladder
A stone has entered the ureter
The inflammation has reached the parietal peritoneum, consistent with appendicitis
The bowel has obstructed
quiz.why: Migration from periumbilical visceral pain to sharp localized RLQ pain is the classic appendicitis sequence, driven by irritation of the body-wall peritoneum. Gallbladder refers to the right scapula, a ureteral stone radiates flank to groin, and obstruction produces distention with no passage of stool or gas.

quiz.q: Which structure, when torn, is most likely to cause rapid hemorrhagic shock with no external bleeding?
choices: The spleen
The gallbladder
The sigmoid colon
The urinary bladder
quiz.why: The spleen is a solid, blood-filled organ and bleeds massively when torn. The gallbladder, colon and bladder are hollow organs whose rupture causes spillage and peritonitis rather than exsanguination.

quiz.q: A 58-year-old with cirrhosis vomits a basin of bright red blood, is pale and diaphoretic with a pulse of 128 and a BP of 92/60. What is your first priority?
choices: Obtain a complete SAMPLE history
Place him supine with legs elevated
Give small sips of water to clear the airway
Suction and position him to protect the airway
quiz.why: Active hematemesis threatens the airway before it threatens the circulation, so suction and drainage positioning come first. History waits, supine risks aspiration in an actively vomiting patient, and nothing goes by mouth.

quiz.q: Black, tarry stool in a patient who has been taking ibuprofen daily most likely indicates:
choices: Hemorrhoidal bleeding
A bleeding peptic ulcer
Diverticulitis
Ovarian cyst rupture
quiz.why: Melena is digested blood from an upper GI source, and chronic NSAID use is a leading cause of peptic ulcer. Hemorrhoids and diverticular bleeding produce bright red rectal blood, and an ovarian cyst causes pelvic pain, not melena.

quiz.q: A 30-year-old man writhes on the floor with severe right flank pain radiating to his groin and reports blood in his urine. Which finding would most change your concern?
choices: He is 68 years old with a history of hypertension and smoking
He reports a similar episode two years ago
He vomited once before you arrived
He cannot find a comfortable position
quiz.why: In an older patient with vascular risk factors, flank and back pain may be a leaking abdominal aortic aneurysm rather than a stone. A prior identical episode, vomiting and restlessness are all typical of renal colic and do not raise concern.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a correct action for a patient with a left arm dialysis fistula?
choices: Take the blood pressure in the right arm
Start an IV distal to the fistula
Draw blood from the fistula for the hospital
Apply a blood pressure cuff over the fistula to check flow
quiz.why: The fistula limb is off limits for cuffs, IVs and blood draws because compression or puncture can clot the access. Using the opposite arm still gives you the blood pressure you need.

quiz.q: A peritoneal dialysis patient reports abdominal pain and fever, and the drained fluid is cloudy. This most suggests:
choices: Hyperkalemia
Fluid overload
Hypoglycemia
Peritonitis
quiz.why: Cloudy effluent with belly pain and fever is peritonitis, the classic complication of peritoneal dialysis. Hyperkalemia causes weakness and dysrhythmias, fluid overload causes dyspnea and edema, and hypoglycemia causes altered mental status.

quiz.q: Which set of findings best fits hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state rather than diabetic ketoacidosis?
choices: Fruity breath odor with Kussmaul respirations
A 19-year-old ill for eight hours with a glucose of 380
An 81-year-old ill for a week, glucose 940, profoundly obtunded, no ketone breath
Rapid onset after an insulin pump failure
quiz.why: HHS is an older Type 2 patient over days to weeks with extreme hyperglycemia, extreme dehydration, and no ketoacidosis. Fruity breath, Kussmaul breathing, a young Type 1 patient, and pump failure all describe DKA.

quiz.q: Your patient's glucose is 58 mg/dL. She is alert, oriented, and able to swallow. The correct EMT action is:
choices: Withhold all oral intake and transport
Assist with her insulin pen
Give IM glucagon
Give 15-25 g of oral glucose and recheck in about 15 minutes
quiz.why: An alert patient who can swallow and protect the airway gets oral glucose, one standard 15 g tube, with a recheck in 15 minutes. Withholding treats nothing, insulin would lower her sugar further, and glucagon is outside EMT scope in most systems and unnecessary when she can swallow.

quiz.q: A 68-year-old woman is found lethargic in a cold apartment with a temperature of 32.8 C, a heart rate of 42, and non-pitting facial puffiness. She is not shivering. The most likely diagnosis is:
choices: Thyroid storm
Myxedema coma
Addisonian crisis
Diabetic ketoacidosis
quiz.why: Hypothermia without shivering, bradycardia, myxedematous puffiness and coma is severe hypothyroidism. Thyroid storm brings fever above 104 F and tachycardia, Addisonian crisis brings vomiting and hypotension, and DKA brings Kussmaul breathing with ketone breath.

quiz.q: Which statement about Kussmaul respirations is correct?
choices: They are deep and rapid and represent the body compensating for acidosis
They are slow and shallow and indicate respiratory failure
They are a sign of hypoglycemia
They occur in hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state but not DKA
quiz.why: Kussmaul respirations are deep, rapid breaths that blow off carbon dioxide to offset ketoacidosis in DKA. They are not slow, not a hypoglycemia sign, and are absent in HHS because HHS is not ketoacidotic.

quiz.q: A patient with known Addison disease is vomiting, profoundly weak, and hypotensive after three days with the flu. What clue most supports adrenal crisis?
choices: Fruity breath odor
Bilateral crackles
A medical alert bracelet and an emergency hydrocortisone injection in her bag
A blood pressure difference between arms
quiz.why: Patients with adrenal insufficiency are typically prescribed an emergency steroid injection and wear alert jewelry; illness is the classic trigger for crisis. Fruity breath is DKA, crackles suggest heart failure, and an interarm BP difference suggests aortic dissection.

quiz.q: A 9-year-old with sickle cell disease has severe bilateral leg and back pain but normal vital signs and a room-air SpO2 of 98%. The best care is:
choices: Withhold care until pain can be objectively confirmed
Warmth, gentle handling, and transport while believing the reported pain, with oxygen only if he becomes hypoxic
Apply cold packs to the painful limbs
Encourage ambulation to improve circulation
quiz.why: Vaso-occlusive crisis has no confirmatory sign, and these patients are chronically undertreated. At a saturation of 98 percent supplemental oxygen adds nothing, so warmth, gentle handling and prompt transport are the care. Cold triggers further sickling, ambulation increases oxygen demand, and withholding care on the basis of doubt is both wrong and dangerous.

quiz.q: A 5-year-old with sickle cell disease is suddenly pale and tachycardic with a BP of 74/40 and a rapidly enlarging, tender left upper quadrant. This is:
choices: Acute chest syndrome
Splenic sequestration
Priapism
A simple pain crisis
quiz.why: The spleen has trapped a large blood volume, producing hemorrhagic shock with no external bleeding, and young children are most at risk. Acute chest syndrome presents with chest pain, fever and hypoxia; priapism involves the penis; a pain crisis does not cause shock.

quiz.q: Hemophilia A is caused by a deficiency of which clotting factor?
choices: Factor VIII
Factor IX
von Willebrand factor
Factor VII
quiz.why: Hemophilia A, the more common form, is factor VIII deficiency. Factor IX deficiency is hemophilia B, and von Willebrand factor deficiency is a separate and milder disorder.

quiz.q: An 84-year-old on warfarin slipped and struck the back of her head. She is alert and oriented with normal vitals and no complaints. What is the correct disposition?
choices: Refusal is appropriate since she is asymptomatic
Advise her to take ibuprofen for soreness
Recheck her in an hour before deciding
Transport for evaluation because anticoagulation makes delayed intracranial bleeding likely
quiz.why: Anticoagulated head strikes can bleed slowly and silently for hours, so a normal exam does not clear her. Ibuprofen worsens bleeding risk, and waiting an hour in the field wastes the window in which a bleed is survivable.

quiz.q: A woman with a known peanut allergy has hives and is wheezing five minutes after eating. Her BP is 118/72. What is the correct action?
choices: Give epinephrine 0.3 mg IM in the lateral thigh
Give diphenhydramine and monitor for 30 minutes
Withhold epinephrine because her blood pressure is normal
Give albuterol only, since wheezing is the sole respiratory finding
quiz.why: Skin plus respiratory involvement is two body systems, which meets the definition of anaphylaxis regardless of blood pressure. Antihistamines and albuterol do not reverse the process, and waiting for hypotension is how patients die.

quiz.q: The correct pediatric epinephrine auto-injector dose is:
choices: 0.1 mg
0.15 mg IM
0.3 mg IM
quiz.why: The pediatric auto-injector delivers 0.15 mg IM, generally for children about 15-30 kg. 0.3 mg is the adult dose, and the other values are not auto-injector strengths.

quiz.q: Twenty minutes after epinephrine a patient is symptom free and the family wants to refuse transport. The strongest reason to insist on transport is:
choices: The auto-injector must be returned to the hospital
The patient will need a prescription refill
Antihistamines can only be given in the ED
A biphasic reaction can recur 4-12 hours later after the epinephrine wears off
quiz.why: Epinephrine lasts only about 10-20 minutes while the immune reaction continues, and symptoms can return hours later, often when the patient is alone. The other reasons are administrative, not clinical.

quiz.q: Which finding is most immediately life-threatening in an allergic patient?
choices: Hoarseness and a complaint that the throat is closing
Widespread hives
Itchy watery eyes
Nausea and one episode of vomiting
quiz.why: Hoarseness and a sensation of throat closure signal laryngeal swelling and impending airway obstruction, the fastest killer in anaphylaxis. Hives, eye symptoms and vomiting are signs of involvement but not of immediate airway loss.

quiz.q: A 24-year-old has lower abdominal pain, fever, foul vaginal discharge, and walks with a slow shuffle because movement hurts. The most likely condition is:
choices: Mittelschmerz
Ovarian torsion
Pelvic inflammatory disease
Endometriosis
quiz.why: Fever with discharge and pain worsened by movement is PID, an ascending infection of the upper reproductive tract. Mittelschmerz is mild and afebrile, torsion is sudden and one-sided without discharge, and endometriosis is chronic and cyclic.

quiz.q: Which of the following is appropriate when caring for a patient after a sexual assault?
choices: Ask what she was wearing to document the scene fully
Perform a genital exam to document injuries
Encourage her to change clothes so she is comfortable
Document her account in her own words in quotation marks
quiz.why: Quoting the patient preserves an accurate, non-judgmental record. Investigative questioning is not the EMT's role, genital exams are limited to life-threatening bleeding, and changing clothes destroys evidence.

quiz.q: When clothing must be removed from a sexual assault patient, you should:
choices: Cut directly through any tears to make removal easier
Cut around existing tears and place clothing in a paper bag
Seal clothing in a plastic bag to keep it clean
Leave the clothing at the scene for police
quiz.why: Cutting through tears destroys forensic detail and plastic traps moisture that degrades biological evidence, so paper bags are used. Clothing removed during care goes with the patient, transferred and documented.

quiz.q: A non-pregnant 40-year-old is soaking two pads an hour and is dizzy with a pulse of 116. Correct care includes:
choices: Packing the vagina with rolled gauze
Inserting a tampon to control flow
Applying external pads, counting them, and treating for shock
Withholding oxygen until the bleeding is controlled
quiz.why: Nothing is inserted into the vagina prehospital because you cannot see the source, may worsen injury, and could destroy evidence. External pads let you estimate loss while you manage hypovolemia, and oxygen is given as needed.

quiz.q: A 26-year-old is agitated and combative at a party. Which assessment finding would most change your working impression from psychiatric to medical?
choices: He has a history of bipolar disorder
His SpO2 is 84% on room air
He is shouting obscenities
Friends say he has been drinking
quiz.why: Hypoxia causes restlessness and combativeness and is immediately correctable, so a saturation of 84% reframes the call as medical. A psychiatric history does not explain the agitation, shouting is nonspecific, and alcohol does not exclude a medical cause.

quiz.q: Which is the correct way to restrain a violent patient?
choices: Supine, four-point soft restraints secured to the stretcher frame, monitored continuously
Prone with the arms secured behind the back
Seated with the wrists tied to the side rails
Prone between two backboards for full immobilization
quiz.why: Supine four-point restraint on the frame preserves chest expansion and allows continuous monitoring. Prone positions and hog-tying cause positional asphyxia, and side rails move, which can injure the limb or loosen the restraint.

quiz.q: Which patient is at highest immediate risk for suicide?
choices: A 30-year-old who says he sometimes feels hopeless
A 22-year-old with a family history of depression
A 47-year-old who attempted suicide last year, lives alone, and has a loaded firearm at home
A 60-year-old who has been in therapy for 10 years
quiz.why: A prior attempt is the strongest predictor, and a specific plan with immediately available means plus social isolation multiplies the risk. Vague hopelessness, family history alone, and ongoing treatment are lower-acuity findings.

quiz.q: A restrained patient in excited delirium abruptly stops struggling and becomes silent and limp. What is the priority?
choices: Release the restraints since he has calmed
Document that he became cooperative
Continue transport without changes
Check for pulse and breathing and prepare for cardiac arrest
quiz.why: Sudden collapse right after a struggle is the classic fatal pattern in excited delirium, driven by acidosis and hyperthermia. Interpreting it as calm or cooperation costs the patient their life.

quiz.q: A 3-year-old sits upright leaning on his hands, drooling, with a muffled voice and a fever that began four hours ago. What should you do?
choices: Use a tongue blade to inspect the throat
Lay him supine for a better airway assessment
Insert an oropharyngeal airway prophylactically
Keep him calm on a caregiver's lap, give blow-by oxygen, and transport
quiz.why: This is epiglottitis; any oral manipulation or forced positioning can cause complete obstruction. Calm, upright, blow-by oxygen and gentle rapid transport is the only safe approach.

quiz.q: A 2-year-old has had cold symptoms for two days and now has a barking cough and stridor that is worse tonight. He is not drooling and is playful between coughs. This is:
choices: Epiglottitis
Croup
Pertussis
Pneumonia
quiz.why: Gradual onset after a cold, barking cough, inspiratory stridor, night worsening and no drooling is croup. Epiglottitis is sudden with drooling and toxic appearance, pertussis gives paroxysms with a whoop, and pneumonia gives fever with focal crackles.

quiz.q: A 6-week-old has coughing fits so violent she turns dusky, followed by gasping. Her older sibling has had a cough for three weeks. What is most concerning about the infant?
choices: She may have apnea rather than a classic whoop
She will develop stridor
She is at risk for epiglottitis
She needs immediate chest compressions
quiz.why: Infants with pertussis often do not whoop and instead have apnea and cyanosis, which is why they must be monitored continuously. Stridor is an upper airway sign, epiglottitis is unrelated, and compressions are only indicated in arrest.

quiz.q: An 82-year-old is confused after two days of poor appetite. He is afebrile with an SpO2 of 89% and crackles at the right lung base. The most likely cause is:
choices: Croup
Asthma
Pneumonia presenting atypically
Pertussis
quiz.why: Elderly pneumonia often presents as confusion or a fall without fever, and focal crackles with hypoxia localize the problem to one lung region. Croup and pertussis are pediatric infectious pictures, and asthma produces wheezing rather than focal crackles.

quiz.q: A 70-year-old with heart failure wakes at night unable to breathe, has crackles rising from both bases, pink frothy sputum, and a BP of 210/110. Besides oxygen, the most beneficial EMT action is:
choices: Sit him fully upright with legs dependent and apply CPAP if authorized
Lay him supine and elevate the legs
Give him water to thin the secretions
Encourage rapid deep breathing exercises
quiz.why: Upright positioning pools blood away from the lungs and CPAP drives fluid back out of the alveoli, which is the single highest-yield intervention available. Supine positioning and leg elevation increase pulmonary congestion, and oral fluids are contraindicated.

quiz.q: Which set of findings converts severe hypertension from urgency to emergency?
choices: A systolic pressure above 200 alone
A new severe headache with blurred vision and slurred speech
A pulse pressure above 60
A history of not taking medications for a week
quiz.why: Hypertensive emergency is defined by end-organ damage, such as neurologic signs, chest pain, or pulmonary edema, not by the number alone. A high systolic, a wide pulse pressure, and medication noncompliance are common in urgency without organ injury.

quiz.q: A 66-year-old smoker has dull low back and abdominal pain and you feel a pulsating mass above the navel. What should you do?
choices: Palpate repeatedly to measure the mass
Have him walk to the ambulance to save time
Handle him gently, avoid deep palpation, and transport rapidly to a surgical facility
Apply firm pressure over the mass to control possible bleeding
quiz.why: A pulsatile mass suggests an abdominal aortic aneurysm, and pressure or repeated palpation can contribute to rupture. Ambulating the patient increases cardiovascular demand, and pressing on the aorta is never a hemorrhage control technique.

quiz.q: A patient two hours into a large myocardial infarction is hypotensive at 80/48, cool and clammy, with crackles throughout both lung fields. This shock is best classified as:
choices: Hypovolemic shock requiring a rapid fluid bolus
Cardiogenic shock, in which fluids can worsen pulmonary edema
Distributive shock from sepsis
Neurogenic shock from spinal injury
quiz.why: Shock signs combined with wet lungs after an MI indicate pump failure, so volume is not the deficit and adding it floods the lungs further. Hypovolemic shock lacks crackles, septic shock shows fever with warm skin early, and neurogenic shock produces bradycardia with warm dry skin.

scenarios.title: Dispatched: allergic reaction, 28F at a restaurant
scenarios.intro: You are dispatched at 1912 to a busy restaurant for an allergic reaction. Dispatch reports a woman having trouble breathing after eating. Her sister and her husband are with her. Scene is safe; a manager meets you at the door and walks you to a back table.

steps.prompt: A 28-year-old woman is sitting forward in a chair. Her face is puffy, hives cover her neck and chest, and she is wheezing audibly. She says, in short phrases, that her throat feels tight. Her sister says she has a shellfish allergy and the appetizer had shrimp paste in it. She has an epinephrine auto-injector in her purse.

choices.text: Assist her with her epinephrine auto-injector, 0.3 mg IM into the lateral thigh, and apply high-flow oxygen
choices.feedback: Correct. Skin plus respiratory plus borderline hypotension is anaphylaxis several times over. Epinephrine is the only drug that reverses it, and every minute of delay raises mortality.

choices.text: Give her diphenhydramine from the family's supply and reassess in 10 minutes
choices.feedback: Harmful delay. Antihistamines take 30 or more minutes, do nothing for laryngeal swelling, and do nothing for hypotension. This patient can lose her airway in that window.

choices.text: Move her to the ambulance first, then decide on medication
choices.feedback: Moving is reasonable, but not before treatment. Epinephrine takes seconds to give and works within minutes. Give it where she sits.

choices.text: Coach her breathing and apply a nasal cannula at 2 L/min while you gather a history
choices.feedback: Far too passive. Coaching does not open a swelling airway, and 2 L/min will not correct a saturation of 91% in anaphylaxis.

steps.prompt: Five minutes after epinephrine the wheezing has softened, her voice is clearer, and the hives are fading. She says she feels much better and wants to sit up. Her husband asks whether she really needs to go to the hospital, since the appetizer is 'out of her system now.'

choices.text: Explain that epinephrine wears off in about 10-20 minutes and the reaction can return hours later, and recommend transport
choices.feedback: Correct. Naming the mechanism in plain words is the most persuasive thing you can do, and it is medically accurate.

choices.text: Agree she looks fine and begin a refusal
choices.feedback: Dangerous. Resolution after epinephrine is expected and says nothing about the next four hours. A biphasic reaction at home can be worse than the first.

choices.text: Tell the husband it is the patient's decision and stop discussing it
choices.feedback: Deferring to the patient is right, but abandoning the conversation is not. She needs the information to make an informed choice, and giving it is your job.

choices.text: Tell them the law requires transport after epinephrine
choices.feedback: Do not invent authority. Most states do not require it, and a false claim destroys your credibility the moment they check. Use the real clinical reason.

steps.prompt: She agrees to go. In the ambulance, seventeen minutes after the epinephrine, she suddenly says her throat is tightening again. You hear her voice roughen. She looks frightened.

choices.text: Administer a second dose of epinephrine per protocol, apply high-flow oxygen, and request an ALS intercept
choices.feedback: Correct. A second dose is indicated at 5-15 minutes when symptoms recur, and this is a recurrence with hypotension and airway involvement.

choices.text: Increase oxygen and continue driving, since she already had epinephrine
choices.feedback: Insufficient. Oxygen does not open a swollen larynx and epinephrine is repeatable by design. Her pressure is falling.

choices.text: Lay her flat and elevate her legs to raise the blood pressure
choices.feedback: Half right and half harmful. Leg elevation helps distributive shock, but a patient with airway swelling and a respiratory rate of 30 must be allowed to sit up. Never force this patient flat.

choices.text: Give albuterol by nebulizer for the throat tightness
choices.feedback: Wrong target. Albuterol relaxes lower airway smooth muscle; the problem here is upper airway swelling and shock, neither of which albuterol touches.

steps.prompt: The second dose works. Her voice clears, saturation rises to 97%, and the pressure comes back up. You are eight minutes from the emergency department. Her husband, riding in front, asks what he should tell the staff.

choices.text: Give the ED a radio report including the allergen, both epinephrine times and doses, the recurrence, and current vitals
choices.feedback: Correct. The two dose times and the fact of recurrence are the details that determine how long the ED observes her.

choices.text: Report only the current, improved vital signs so the ED is not misled about her present condition
choices.feedback: Incomplete and misleading in the other direction. A patient who recurred once looks deceptively well and needs prolonged observation; the ED must know.

choices.text: Tell the husband the ED will figure it out from your paperwork later
choices.feedback: The written report comes after handoff. Verbal notification before arrival is what gets a bed and a physician ready.

scenarios.debrief: The pattern: anaphylaxis is defined by two or more body systems or hypotension after exposure, and epinephrine is the only treatment that reverses it. Adult 0.3 mg IM lateral thigh, repeat at 5-15 minutes if symptoms persist or recur. Epinephrine lasts roughly 10-20 minutes while the immune reaction continues for hours, which is exactly why a biphasic reaction happens and why every anaphylaxis patient transports. When a family wants to refuse, the persuasive move is the mechanism explained plainly, never a fabricated legal rule.

scenarios.title: Dispatched: 61M, weakness, missed dialysis
scenarios.intro: You are dispatched at 1040 to a private residence for a man with general weakness. Dispatch notes a family member reported he 'hasn't been to his treatments.' Scene is safe. A daughter meets you at the door and says her father has been on dialysis for six years.

steps.prompt: A 61-year-old man sits on the edge of his bed, breathing with visible effort and speaking in three- and four-word sentences. His legs are swollen to mid-calf and his face looks puffy. His daughter says he missed Monday and Wednesday dialysis because his ride fell through. There is a surgical scar and a visible bulge on his left forearm.

choices.text: Sit him fully upright, apply high-flow oxygen, and take the blood pressure in the right arm
choices.feedback: Correct on all three. He is fluid overloaded, upright positioning and oxygen are the interventions you have, and the left forearm holds his fistula, which is off limits for cuffs.

choices.text: Lay him supine to assess lung sounds and take the blood pressure in the left arm
choices.feedback: Two harms at once. Supine floods the lungs further in fluid overload, and cuffing the fistula arm risks clotting the access he depends on to stay alive.

choices.text: Apply oxygen by nasal cannula at 2 L/min and begin the history
choices.feedback: Too little oxygen for a saturation of 89% with work of breathing. Position and oxygen delivery both need to be more aggressive.

choices.text: Assume anxiety and coach his breathing while you look for medications
choices.feedback: This is not anxiety. Swollen legs, a puffy face, hypoxia and two missed dialysis sessions point squarely at fluid overload.

steps.prompt: You hear crackles from the bases up through the mid fields bilaterally. He tells you, slowly, that he also feels 'weak all over' and that his legs have been cramping and tingling since yesterday. His daughter asks if this is just his usual shortness of breath.

choices.text: Recognize that generalized weakness, cramps and tingling after missed dialysis suggest hyperkalemia, and treat him as a high-acuity cardiac risk
choices.feedback: Correct. Potassium builds without dialysis and causes lethal rhythms with almost no warning. This changes him from a breathing problem to a potential arrest.

choices.text: Attribute the cramps to dehydration and offer him water
choices.feedback: Backwards. He is volume overloaded, not dry, and oral fluid adds to the problem. Nothing by mouth is appropriate.

choices.text: Note the symptoms and continue routine transport at low priority
choices.feedback: Underestimates him. Missed dialysis plus diffuse weakness is a recognized pre-arrest pattern that warrants urgency and ALS.

choices.text: Have him walk to the stretcher in the hallway to save time
choices.feedback: Do not exert this patient. Exertion increases oxygen demand in a hypoxic, potentially dysrhythmic patient. Carry him.

steps.prompt: You request an ALS intercept and move him to the ambulance. While you secure the stretcher, the dressing over his left forearm soaks through and bright red blood begins running steadily from the fistula site.

choices.text: Apply firm, focused direct pressure with a gloved fingertip over gauze at the bleeding point and hold it
choices.feedback: Correct. Fistula bleeding is under near-arterial pressure and responds to focal, sustained pressure. Holding without peeking is what stops it.

choices.text: Wrap the forearm tightly with a circumferential elastic bandage
choices.feedback: A circumferential wrap tight enough to stop this bleeding will clot the access and may not stop it anyway. Use focal pressure.

choices.text: Apply a tourniquet above the elbow immediately
choices.feedback: Too far, too soon. A tourniquet destroys the access and is reserved for bleeding that is uncontrollable and life-threatening after direct pressure has failed.

choices.text: Cover it with a bulky dressing and check it every few minutes
choices.feedback: Bulky dressings spread the force instead of concentrating it, and lifting to check restarts the bleeding. Hold focal pressure continuously.

steps.prompt: Bleeding is controlled with sustained pressure. He remains upright on high-flow oxygen with a saturation of 95%. ALS is meeting you in four minutes at a highway pull-off.

choices.text: Give the paramedic a report naming the two missed sessions, the weakness and cramping, the crackles, the fistula bleed and how it was controlled
choices.feedback: Correct. The missed sessions plus the neuromuscular symptoms are what will drive their treatment for suspected hyperkalemia.

choices.text: Report only the respiratory complaint, since that is what he called for
choices.feedback: Omits the most dangerous piece. Without the dialysis history and the weakness, the crew may treat only the breathing and miss the potassium.

choices.text: Hand over the patient and let the paramedic read your chart on scene
choices.feedback: A verbal handoff is faster and safer than a chart, especially when the key facts are historical rather than visible on exam.

scenarios.debrief: The pattern: a dialysis patient who missed sessions has two clocks running. Fluid overload is the one you see, treated with upright positioning, oxygen, and CPAP if your agency carries it. Hyperkalemia is the one you cannot see, announced only by vague weakness, cramping and tingling, and ending in a lethal rhythm without warning. Always ask when the last treatment was and whether it was completed. The fistula arm gets no cuff, no IV, no blood draw, and a bleeding fistula is controlled with focused fingertip pressure, not a wrap and not a tourniquet.
